props.title: The Boy Friend
props.initialSlug: Twiggy stars in dazzling '20s musical tribute

sections.content: Ken Russell's The Boy Friend represents a fascinating meta-theatrical adaptation of Sandy Wilson's 1954 stage musical. Set in a run-down English theater during the 1920s, the film stars Twiggy in her screen debut as Polly Browne, an assistant stage manager forced to take the lead role when the star breaks her ankle. Russell transforms the simple musical into a dazzling commentary on performance itself, alternating between the shabby "real" theater production and lavish Busby Berkeley-style fantasy sequences. The film draws clear inspiration from classic Hollywood musicals like 42nd Street (1933) and Gold Diggers of 1933 (1933), while maintaining Russell's signature experimental flair.

sections.content: Russell's direction creates fascinating layers of reality and fantasy, much like his later film Tommy (1975). The musical numbers shift between the cramped stage performance and elaborate dream sequences that channel both Art Deco glamour and psychedelic 1970s aesthetics. Twiggy proves surprisingly capable in her acting debut, bringing an authentic vulnerability to Polly while handling the singing and dancing with unexpected skill. The film serves as a bridge between classical Hollywood musicals and the more experimental fare of the 1970s, like Cabaret (1972) and That's Entertainment! (1974).

The production design deserves special attention for its dual nature - the authentic grit of the struggling theater contrasts beautifully with the surreal fantasy sequences. This approach influenced later meta-musicals like All That Jazz (1979) and Pennies from Heaven (1981), where reality and fantasy collide. Russell's characteristic excess works perfectly within the musical genre, allowing him to indulge his most flamboyant impulses while still serving the story's themes about the transformative power of performance. sections.content: The Boy Friend helped establish a new sub-genre of self-aware musicals that commented on the form itself. This influence can be seen in films like Pennies from Heaven (1981), The Producers (1967), and more recently La La Land (2016). The film's exploration of the relationship between theatrical and cinematic space created a template for later works that played with similar concepts, such as Moulin Rouge! (2001) and Chicago (2002).
